data.summary: configwrite._toml_literal (also review._toml_value, companions json.dumps path) quotes strings with json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True), which writes a character outside the BMP (e.g. an emoji) as a UTF-16 surrogate pair \ud83d\ude80; TOML \u escapes must be Unicode scalar values, so tomllib refuses the file. Probe 2026-10-05: tomllib.loads('x = ' + _toml_literal('ship it 🚀')) -> TOMLDecodeError 'Escaped character is not a Unicode scalar value'. So 'ddflow config <key> <value with emoji>' writes a config that no later command can read. Fix: one TOML basic-string writer (ensure_ascii=False, escape U+007F) used by every writer.
data.title: TOML string writers emit surrogate escapes for non-BMP characters, producing unparseable TOML

data.body:
Fixes bug Bb11e7a8186: configwrite._toml_literal (also review._toml_value, companions json.dumps path) quotes strings with json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True), which writes a character outside the BMP (e.g. an emoji) as a UTF-16 surrogate pair \ud83d\ude80; TOML \u escapes must be Unicode scalar values, so tomllib refuses the file. Probe 2026-10-05: tomllib.loads('x = ' + _toml_literal('ship it 🚀')) -> TOMLDecodeError 'Escaped character is not a Unicode scalar value'. So 'ddflow config <key> <value with emoji>' writes a config that no later command can read. Fix: one TOML basic-string writer (ensure_ascii=False, escape U+007F) used by every writer.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-Bb11e7a8186 --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed Bb11e7a8186 --regression-test <test>` first).
data.title: Fix bug Bb11e7a8186: TOML string writers emit surrogate escapes for non-BMP characters, producing unparseable TOML

data.claim: No: _toml_literal (json.dumps, ensure_ascii=True) is not a correct TOML string writer for arbitrary text: it leaves values like 'true' or '[x]' unquoted, and writes non-BMP chars as surrogate pairs TOML refuses; json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False) plus escaping U+007F round-trips every string.
data.falsifier: tomllib.loads('x = '+_toml_literal('ship it 🚀')) parses, or json.dumps(s, ensure_ascii=False) round-trips U+007F
data.mechanism: TOML \u escapes must be Unicode scalar values; TOML forbids raw U+007F in basic strings; _toml_literal passes through anything that looks like a TOML literal
data.probe: uv run python -c tomllib.loads('x = '+_toml_literal('ship it 🚀')); and json.dumps(ch, ensure_ascii=False) for 🚀, \x7f, é
data.probe_output: _toml_literal: ERR Escaped character is not a Unicode scalar value (line 1 col 20). ensure_ascii=True: 🚀 ERR, \x7f ok; ensure_ascii=False: 🚀 ok, \x7f ERR Illegal character. Unfixed Rule.to_toml: 10 of 16 round-trip cases failed (TOMLDecodeError line 2 col 15 for say "hi").
data.question: Can configwrite._toml_literal be reused as the escaper for Rule.to_toml string fields?

A config FILE carrying one is treated like an unknown knob: recorded in unknown_knobs, warned on stderr, reported by doctor, and the knob keeps its default -- all KNOB_CHOICES knobs are in _TOLERANT_VALUES.

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff replaces `_TOLERANT_VALUES = frozenset({"mcp.tools", "export.refresh", "export.tables"})` with `frozenset({*KNOB_CHOICES, "export.tables"})`, i.e. it makes *every* newly-validated enum knob tolerant. Per the surviving code comment, a tolerant knob's value in a config FILE "is skipped with a warning rather than refused". So the file-load path reintroduces exactly the failure this bug is about: with a config file containing

    [enforce]
    stale_docs = "blok"

the value is no longer refused (a check now exists, but it is bypassed for tolerant knobs); it is skipped with a warning and the knob falls back to its default, i.e. the misspelt policy still "quietly behaves as some other value". The fix only refuses on the write path (`Config.check` / `config set`), which is the exact probe in the report, so a test that only calls `Config.check` will pass while the actual file-driven behavior remains. It is also a concrete behavioral regression for at least `dedupe.on_match`, which the intent states was previously refused on load (`_KNOB_CHECKS`-checked and *not* tolerant); after this change it is in `KNOB_CHOICES`, therefore in `_TOLERANT_VALUES`, so an invalid `dedupe.on_match` in a config file is downgraded from a hard refusal to a warning-plus-default. The original comment scoped tolerance to knobs "whose VALUE set can grow in a later release"; fixed domains such as `enforce.*` (`block | warn | off`) and `dedupe.on_match` do not qualify, so blanket tolerance defeats the stated guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config.py: _TOLERANT_VALUES

chunk_findings.detail: In a dict display, later keys overwrite earlier ones, so putting the derived block last means every knob that appears both in `KNOB_CHOICES` and in the hand-written table loses its hand-written validator. The entry immediately above the spread, `dedupe.kinds`, is exactly one of the enum knobs this change is meant to cover: its allowed values are the enumerated `DEDUPE_KINDS`, so it is a natural member of `KNOB_CHOICES`. Its hand-written check is list-aware (`isinstance(v, list) and all(x in DEDUPE_KINDS for x in v)`), but once the spread is expanded after it, `_one_of(DEDUPE_KINDS)` takes precedence and performs scalar membership. A valid config such as `dedupe.kinds = ["plan"]` is then tested as `["plan"] in DEDUPE_KINDS`, which is `False`, so a legal value is reported as "must be one of ..." and refused; the list branch becomes dead code. The regression test described in the intent only asserts that *bad* values are refused, so it will not catch this — it happily passes while valid list-valued knobs are rejected. The derived block needs to be expanded before the hand-written entries (or overlapping keys excluded), otherwise any future/present overlap silently downgrades a specialized validator to a scalar one.

chunk_findings.detail: The final assertion in the rewritten test is `assert A.check_after_merge(repo, sha=sha).get("status") != "unavailable"`. Using `.get(...)` makes the test pass whenever the key is absent, and the `!= "unavailable"` form passes for any other value, so the test no longer pins down that the merge actually proceeds with the default `fast` mode after an unknown enum value. Concrete failure: if `check_after_merge` regresses to return `{}` (or `{"status": "error", ...}`) for a config whose `ci.on_merge` value was `"sometimes"`, `.get("status")` yields `None` (or `"error"`), which is `!= "unavailable"`, so this test still passes even though the merge did not run as intended. The test is supposed to prove the unknown knob falls back to the default and the merge proceeds, so it should assert the concrete success status/payload (e.g. the same status a valid `on_merge = "fast"` produces) rather than a negation. The preceding `Config.load`/`Config.check` assertions do not compensate, because they only exercise config parsing, not the `check_after_merge` outcome.

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes *every* enumerated knob tolerant by deriving `_TOLERANT_VALUES` from `KNOB_CHOICES`, but the comment on `_TOLERANT_VALUES` says a tolerant knob found in a config *file* with an unknown value "is skipped with a warning rather than refused". That directly undercuts the stated purpose of the fix ("a misspelt policy quietly behaves as some other value" → "a bad value is refused"), because the file-load path never refuses any of the newly-declared enums; it silently drops the misspelt policy and falls back to the default. Concrete input: a config file containing `[flow]\nmodel = "trunkk"` now loads with `flow.model` reverted to the default (`trunk`) with only a warning, so the user's intended switch to `gitflow` is silently lost. Worse, this is a strict regression for knobs that were already checked and were *not* tolerant before this diff — `dedupe.on_match` was in `_KNOB_CHECKS` and absent from `_TOLERANT_VALUES`, so a file with `[dedupe]\non_match = "x"` previously failed loudly; after this change `dedupe.on_match` is in `_TOLERANT_VALUES`, so the same file loads and the value is dropped (the exact "silent-knob-drop class" the removed comment warned about). The new regression test only exercises `Config.check` (the write path, which still refuses), so it passes while the file path that produced the original bug report remains unvalidated.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_alternatives` strips every parenthesised group out of the text *before* looking for the `a | b | c` run:

```python
m = re.search(_ALTS, re.sub(r"\s*\([^)]*\)", "", text))
```

so a knob whose allowed values are themselves written as a parenthesised enumeration is silently dropped. Concretely, `_alternatives("(block | warn | off)")` returns `None` (the `re.sub` deletes the whole string, then `re.search` finds nothing), even though the text plainly contains the `block | warn | off` run the function claims to return; `_alternatives("(block | warn) also off | auto")` returns `("off", "auto")`, silently losing `block` and `warn`. Any knob documented as `# (block | warn | off)` is therefore absent from `LISTED`, which means `test_a_value_outside_the_listed_alternatives_is_refused` is never parametrised for it and `Config.check` is never exercised with a bad value for that knob. If the fix forgets/mis-declares the choices for such a knob, this regression suite still passes: the only guard is `test_the_scan_finds_the_knobs_the_bug_named`, which hard-codes six key names and `len(LISTED) >= 21`, so a parser miss can be masked by other knobs. The same hole exists for alternatives written in quotes (`"a" | "b"`, which `_ALTS` cannot match because `"` is not in `[\w-]`) or separated by commas (`a, b, c`); these are exactly the “knob whose allowed values are only written in a comment” cases the change is supposed to catch, and the test docstring’s claim that such a knob “fails here too” holds only when the comment happens to use a bare, unquoted, unparenthesised `a | b | c`.
